attributes.body:
As a particle, が has several different uses in Japanese. However, each of these different uses share a common theme. That theme expresses 'highlighting (A) as important, (B)'. In this use, が comes across as 'but', or 'however' in English.

This nuance of が is used directly after any form of verb or い-Adjective, but requires one of the conjugations of だ or です before it when used with a noun or な-Adjective.

From these examples, we can see that が is simply highlighting that 'while (A) is important, there is extra information'. が with the meaning of 'but' is considered to be very formal, this is due to it sounding quite direct in asserting that there is extra information.

Caution

Sometimes a statement will end with が. In these cases it just means that more information exists, but it is obvious, so it does not need to be said.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: The Conjunctive Particles が & けれど

attributes.body: ものの expresses contrast, similar to 'although' in English, showing that while one thing is true, another contradicts it. が also expresses contrast, but its nuance is weaker, and in some cases, it merely introduces a statement without implying contrast. が is more general, while ものの is more specific. Both are formal and more common in writing than in casual speech.

Both express contrast, but が is more formal and used in writing, like 面白いが難しい ('It's interesting, but difficult'). When combined with ～んだ・～んです, as in 行きたいんですが, it softens the sentence and invites a response or action from the listener.

Both が and けれども express contrast, similar to 'but' in English, or sometimes simply indicate a transition to added information (like 'and'). Both are somewhat formal, used in writing or formal speech, compared to the casual けど. Note that while が and けれども follow immediately after verbs or い-Adjectives, だ or です is required after a な-Adjective or noun.

Both ところが and が express contrast or contradiction. ところが is used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize a contrast between expectation and reality. In contrast, が is used after a phrase or at the end of a sentence to express simple contrast, or sometimes to add information or context without implying surprise or expectation.

second_relatable.title: ところが
second_relatable.meaning: Even so, However, Even though, But

attributes.body: The particle が in both patterns expresses contrast, similar to 'but' in English, or sometimes indicates a transition to additional information (like 'and'). The difference is that が follows directly after an い-Adjective or verb, while it requires だ or です after a な-Adjective or noun. が is somewhat formal and often used in writing or formal speech.

くせに expresses disapproval, similar to 'in spite of' or 'although' in English. In contrast, が is a neutral connecting particle, often expressing contrast (like 'but') or adding information (like 'and'). Unlike くせに, which carries a negative nuance, が is neutral. After な-Adjectives and nouns, くせに requires な or の, while が requires だ or です.

Both が (or だが/ですが after a noun or な-adjective) and けど・だけど express contrast or transition, similar to 'but' in English (e.g., '見た目は美味しそうだけど、味がない' = 'It looks tasty, but has no flavor'). The difference is that が is more formal or written-style, while けど is more colloquial. Both can also be used at the end of a sentence to suggest an implied contrast, even if not explicitly stated.
